title: Carney says Albertans should vote ‘No to the Nine’ in referendum
summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans should vote against the nine referendum questions focused on immigration and constitutional reform as he visited Calgary on Thursday.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre, meets and greets volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Mike Sturk/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans should vote against the nine referendum questions focused on immigration and constitutional reform as he visited Calgary on Thursday.
Alberta premier says it appears PM has yet to fully understand 'damaging' policies of predecessor
"I just wanted to come here, thank you for what you've already done, thank you what you're going to do in the next few days," Carney told the crowd in the city's northeast.
"Make sure everyone's out there marking their ballots ... including, 'No to the Nine.'"
"No to the Nine" is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine ballot questions on Oct. 19, in addition to voting to remain in Canada.

blocks.text: Carney was meeting with volunteers and others at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary.
Earlier, he appeared to discuss the campaign with a person holding a sign tied to a campaign from Public Interest Alberta, an education advocacy group.
"'No on the Nine' … that's good," Carney said.
Carney says 'No to the 9' while campaigning for Canadian unity in Calgary
In a response posted on X, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith wrote that she and Carney have found common ground on many things over the last 18 months.
"However, it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were," Smith wrote.
"Those policies caused Canada’s cost of living to skyrocket, overwhelmed our social services, and made homes and jobs unattainable for thousands of young Canadians.
"That’s why I’m encouraging Albertans to vote ‘yes to the rest’"

blocks.text: The prime minister has previously spoken out on the separatism question. In a Thanksgiving message delivered from a classroom in Edmonton, Carney highlighted various federal initiatives, such as the Pacific Link pipeline.
"We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines," Carney said.

Carney is scheduled to join former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for his Forever Canadian group Thursday evening, while Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver a pro-unity message at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Friday.
Carney is also expected to attend a rally on Friday at a Red Deer brewery with Smith, as well as make a stop in Edmonton the same day.

blocks.text: Volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park hold placards for Alberta's referendum during a visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)
Smith, while saying she has voted to remain in Canada, has advocated for Albertans to vote "yes" to the other nine questions.
Speaking to CBC News' chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault during a one-on-one interview in Calgary last week, Smith said the nine questions are those which she "wants a mandate" on.
"I haven't been neutral on that," Smith said. "I've been persuading people that this is what we need to do."
Earlier this week, three former Alberta premiers urged voters to say "no" to the five immigration-related questions on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot.
In a statement, a spokesperson in the Prime Minister's Office wrote that Canada's government "believes in co-operative federalism that can deliver for Albertans on the issues that matter to them."

"We work continuously with the Province of Alberta on shared priorities addressing areas of concern through established processes — without needing to have a referendum that divides us at a time when we need to be strong, and we are stronger together."
Carney was also asked about his position on the nine questions while speaking on Thursday with Rishi Nagar, a host on the Calgary radio station Red FM.
"Well, the first thing is that we don't need a referendum to make progress on taking control on immigration. We've taken control on immigration," Carney said.

Carney also told Global News on Thursday morning that his government has taken back control of immigration, pointing to declines in asylum seekers, temporary foreign workers and international students.
“We’ve increased the number of economic migrants and we’re increasing the co-operation with the provinces in terms of those selections,” he said.
"To be candid, I don't need a referendum to tell us to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration — I think that’s where we’re headed,” he said.
"I think we're going to get there irrespective of the result" on the referendum questions.
CBC News has requested additional comment from the Alberta premier's office.
Liberal MP says he's voting against questions
Liberal MP Corey Hogan, who represents a Calgary riding, spoke to CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener on Thursday about the nine other questions.
Hogan said he was voting "no" to the entire process.
"We should be asking ourselves: do we want to reward this kind of behaviour? And I don't think that we should," Hogan said.
"I don't think that we should use our country as a bargaining chip … I think the questions are quite manipulative — they're written in ways to get certain answers."

Although he said he'd vote "no" to all nine questions as a sort of protest to the process, he was most open to Question 7, which involves abolishing the federal Senate.
"With all love to my senator colleagues: I love senators; I don't love the Senate," he said.
